general_information.Description: This course provides knowledge of all basic sociological research methods as well as understanding of specific communication research and assessment instruments. As a result, the students will gain a practical understanding of research, evaluation in academic and professional settings. The course program includes practical acquaintance with contemporary media and social networks monitoring systems. Note: I. Prohibit all forms of copyright infringement, and plagiarism in all ideas, documents and media productions and fraud during the course including all ongoing tests and final examinations. A plagiarism percentage of more than 20 per cent (checked by Turnitin) indicates that a student plagiarised with the intent to cheat. II. Recomments: AI tools can be useful educational tools when employed properly A. AI tools are generally acceptable for: 1. Generating ideas through brainstorming 2. Proofreading and conducting grammar checks 3. Clarifying complex ideas 4. Creating practice questions 5. Arranging research notes 6. Data visualization (in reference to AI tools) 7. Image or video creations (in reference to AI tools) Content generated by AI tools must be referenced. Any work generated by AI without the appropriate reference will be considered a cheat attempt and assessed on a case-by-case basis. B. AI tools are not recommended for: 1. Complete assignments or exams that are intended to evaluate your knowledge. 2. Creating essays or reports on your behalf 3. Bypassing the development of research skills
general_information.StudentTasks: - Attend at least 80% of contact hours in order to be accepted to the final examination - Actively participate in class activities - Fulfil tasks given by instructor after class - Use their own laptop in class only for learning purpose - Read the textbook in advance

learning_outcomes.CLO Details: To explain the nature of research in communication field and its process with different steps.
To distinguish different research methods in communication and select the most appropriate one for their research problems.
To apply qualitative research methods in communication field.
To apply quantitative research methods in communication field.
To create report and presentation to communicate their research project
To design and conduct a communication research project; ensuring validity and reliablity and avoiding ethical issues.
To respect research ethics and conduct communication research in an ethical way

assessments.Note: Participation grade will be given based on students' attendance, preparation, and quantity as well as quality of participation in classroom; quality of participation is demonstrated through asking relevant questions, making statements that add to and facilitate class discussion, and builds upon others’ comments.

assessments.Question Type: This is a group-based project. Each group of 4-6 members work together to select a research topic in communication area and submit a research proposal to lecturer and other classmates.;
assessments.Knowledge and Skill: Based on topics of studied units;
assessments.Note: This assignment has 2 components: Research Proposal + PPT slide for oral presentation. - At the end of the proposal, students are required to write a short exlanation about how they apply AI (10%). This criterion follows the instructions below. + Students are permitted to use in-built generative AI such as research paper summary, literature review editing, seaching secondary data but are required to generate their own responses in line with conditions and expectations of the task. + At the end of this assigment, students are required to write a short paragragh (150-200 words) about how they use AI. + Students provide screenshot as evidence of using AI All assignments should be typed and double-spaced with 12-point font, and must be submitted in soft copy. A deduction of 10% of the assignment mark will be applied for each day of late submission.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ1.1
constructive_questions.Details: Find an article in the New York Times based on a scholarly article that deals with social science research on media. Analyze the article and answer the following questions: 1. What methodology was used in the research? 2. How important is the topic? 3. What conclusions were reached? 4. Are the conclusions supported by the data? Are the conclusions credible? 5. Can one generalize from the research? 6. Do the findings have any policy implications?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ2.1
constructive_questions.Details: Investigate smartphones. What have scholars found about the impact smartphones have on Vietnamese culture and society? Deal with topics such as smartphones and the socialization of young people and smartphones and politics. On a personal level, which smartphone do you think is “best” for the typical student? What brand and model of smart phone do you have, and why did you decide to purchase it? If you could afford to purchase any cell phone, which brand and model would you choose?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ3.1
constructive_questions.Details: Using the library and the Internet’s access to scholarly journals, find articles that deal with the following topics: The relation between modernism and postmodernism Suicide rates in various countries International tourism (how many people go to the top 10 countries) Advertising expenditures in the United States, France, Germany, Japan, China, and Brazil The cultural significance of James Bond movies. Lecture can select other case studies for this question.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ4.1
constructive_questions.Details: Apply Chaim Eyal’s list of questions and other things you’ve learned from this book to ask about research to an article that uses survey research.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ8.1
constructive_questions.Details: Find an advertisement that has both metaphor and metonymy and explain how they function to sell the product. Study the facial expressions of the people in the advertisement. What do you think they reveal? On what basis do you come to your conclusions?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ9.1
constructive_questions.Details: Record and review a television commercial and discuss the signs and other aspects of the commercial that you found interesting. Use an applications chart to list the semiotic terms you used in your analysis and to show how you have applied them. Make a syntagmatic (Propp) and paradigmatic (Lévi-Strauss) analysis of the text.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ10.1
constructive_questions.Details: Using the terms in the miniglossary of common rhetorical devices and the analysis of the Sea to Skin advertisement as a model, make a 1,000-word rhetorical analysis of an advertisement that has a large number of words and many rhetorical devices in it. Use the applications chart format to list the concepts and their applications to the advertisement on the first page. Turn in the advertisement with your paper.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ11.1
constructive_questions.Details: How would you characterize Musil’s style of writing? Do you like his style? Explain your answer

constructive_questions.Name: CQ12.1
constructive_questions.Details: Make a rhetorical analysis of the lyrics of a popular song. Use an applications chart in your analysis.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ13.1
constructive_questions.Details: You are appointed media critic for the Marxist journal Arts/Comrade. Using the most important concepts from Marxist theory, write a 1,000-word Marxist interpretation of the film The Hunger Games or one that your instructor assigns. Use the applications chart format described earlier. Which of the four political cultures does The Hunger Games or the film you review appeal to most? Explain your answer.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ14.1
constructive_questions.Details: Using Marxist concepts, write a 1,000-word analysis for Arts/Comrade of “The General” episode of The Prisoner. You can find this episode on the Internet and see it at no cost. Use the applications chart format. Is a psychoanalytic or semiotic analysis of this episode a better approach?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ15.1
constructive_questions.Details: Find an advertisement that uses sexuality to sell a product. Offer a 1,000- to 1,500-word psychoanalytic interpretation of the symbolism, language, and other matters for Psyche magazine. Use an applications chart for the first page of your analysis. Turn in the advertisement with your paper.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ16.1
constructive_questions.Details: Using scholarly journals, investigate psychoanalytic studies of horror as a genre and of a particular horror film, television show, or video. What does the recent popularity of horror texts in all media say about American culture? Why were Buffy, the Vampire Slayer and Twilight such big hits? Why are vampires so interesting to audiences? Do women relate differently from men to vampire stories?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ17.1
constructive_questions.Details: Using the discussion of the Kenneth Cole advertisement as a model, make a critical discourse analysis of a print advertisement that has images and text you find intriguing.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ18.1
constructive_questions.Details: Make a critical, multimodal analysis of a popular music video on YouTube. Discuss the language used in the song and the nature of the dancing. What problems did you face in making your analysis?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ19.1
constructive_questions.Details: Write a narrative of three or four sentences and then rewrite it in six different styles. What did you learn from this exercise?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ25.1
constructive_questions.Details: An alien arrives from Mars in a spaceship. You are a reporter for a major television news show. Prepare a list of key interview questions to ask the Martian and a list of follow-up questions. Explain your rationale for asking each question. What problems did you face in making your list of interview questions? How do your questions solve these problems? You can practice interviewing this Martian with someone in your class to get a sense of the difficulties one faces in conducting an interview.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ26.1
constructive_questions.Details: The president of the United States grants you an interview but says you can only ask 10 questions. What questions would you ask him or her? How did you decide on your questions? Compare your list of questions with those asked by other members of your class. Are there any questions that everyone asked? Any surprising questions? Any important questions that should have been asked?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ27.1
constructive_questions.Details: Tape a television interview and analyze the questions the interviewer asked, questions that should have been asked, and other topics dealt with in this chapter. Observe things such as facial expressions, body language, the tone of the interview, and the relationship between the interviewer and person being interviewed.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ28.1
constructive_questions.Details: Investigate reviews of the writings of historian Arnold Toynbee. Compare reviews in newspapers and popular magazines with reviews in scholarly journals. What differences of opinion do you find in the two kinds of publications about Toynbee’s status as a historian?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ29.1
constructive_questions.Details: Do a research project on new trends in historical analysis. What new approaches have historians come up with in recent years? Why have they developed these approaches?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ30.1
constructive_questions.Details: Using Garfinkel’s method, in which you pretend you are a boarder, write a detailed description of a meal with your family or some friends. Describe what happened as carefully as you can, assuming you don’t know the people and without making any assumptions about their motives.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ31.1
constructive_questions.Details: Find a transcript for a situation comedy such as Modern Family or The Big Bang Theory and analyze the conversation from an ethnomethodological perspective. What assumptions do the characters have about one another and about life? Are there any behavioral codes that inform the dialogue?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ32.1
constructive_questions.Details: Make an ethnomethodological analysis of song lyrics with interesting metaphors or metonymies. Use the “love is a game” analysis as a model.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ33.1
constructive_questions.Details: Using the techniques of humor chart, analyze a joke or other comic text. I offer the following texts for you to practice this kind of analysis: A person calls Radio Erevan and asks, “Is it true that comrade Gorshinko won 5,000 rubles at the lottery?” “Yes,” replies Radio Erevan. “But it was not comrade Gorshinko but comrade Kataev, and it was not 5,000 rubles but 10,000 rubles, and he didn’t win it at the lottery but lost it gambling.” A person calls Radio Erevan and asks, “Is it true that one can use a glass of water for birth control?” “Yes,” replies Radio Erevan. “Before or after?” asks the caller. “Instead of,” replies Radio Erevan. Jack eating rotten cheese did say, Like Samson I my thousands slay; I vow, quoth Roger, so you do. And with the self-same weapon, too.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ34.1
constructive_questions.Details: Taking the role of participant observer, observe the behavior of people at a restaurant or cafeteria. Answer questions listed in the book about things we hope to learn from making a participant observation and use the list of significant considerations as well. What problems did you face in making your analysis? How did you solve these problems?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ35.1
constructive_questions.Details: Take a series of photographs from your typical day, from the time you get up in the morning until you go to bed. When you look at these photographs, do you find anything that reveals some aspect of your life you were unaware of? When you compare your photographs with those your classmates have made of their typical days, do you discover anything the images have in common? Do you find any surprising differences between them?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ37.1
constructive_questions.Details: Using the list of oppositions in kinds of violence, make a content analysis of the kinds of violence found in an episode of a crime television show. Prepare a coding sheet for the analysis. Did you find anything surprising in your analysis? If you can find an episode of the show done a number of years earlier, you can see whether there have been any changes in the way violence is used.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ38.1
constructive_questions.Details: Make a content analysis of the words spoken by males and females in a newspaper’s comic strip page on one weekday in 1995 and one weekday in 2015. Base your analysis on the step-by-step content analysis list and coding sheet from this chapter. What problems did you face in making your content analysis? What were your findings? Did they surprise you in any way? You can also study other topics in the comics, such as the kinds of violence found in them, the number of male and female figures found in them, and so on.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ39.1
constructive_questions.Details: Find three magazine articles about “idols of production” (e.g., political figures, businesspersons) and three about “idols of consumption” (e.g., movie stars, entertainers, celebrities). Duplicate the first pages of the articles and bring them to class. What problems did you face in finding your “idols”? What interesting things did you find in the articles? Where did you go looking for idols of production?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ40.1
constructive_questions.Details: Using your classmates as your universe, prepare a questionnaire about the amount of television, radio, video games, and other media they use in a typical day. Also find out their cell phone and MP3 player usage during a typical day. Use the discussion of writing survey questions to create your survey. What are the most important things you want to find out? How can you avoid confusing questions, showing bias, obtaining incorrect information, or embarrassing those answering the questionnaire? Later, in class, compare the first five questions asked in each questionnaire.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ41.1
constructive_questions.Details: Find a scholarly article that uses surveys and analyze the questions it asks. Do you find any problems with the questions? If so, explain. Could you have asked better questions? If so, write them down for classroom discussion. What problems did the writers of the survey face when designing it? How did they overcome them?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ42.1
constructive_questions.Details: Using a web survey program such as SurveyMonkey, conduct a survey about a topic of interest to you or assigned by your instructor. Pay attention to the way you frame your questions to ensure you obtain valuable information.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ43.1
constructive_questions.Details: Critique an article in a scholarly journal on media and communication that describes an experiment. Use the checklist on experimental design in your discussion of the article. Make a copy of the first page of the article to turn in with your analysis.

constructive_questions.Name: CQ44.1
constructive_questions.Details: Design a simple experiment involving media effects that you can make with your classmates, with half of them as the control group and the other half as the group involved in the experiment. What do you want to find out? How will you discover what you want to find out? What problems do you face in conducting this experiment? Compare the experiments your classmates created to see if there are any commonalities among them. Did anyone have an experimental idea that strikes you as truly ingenious?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ45.1
constructive_questions.Details: Investigate the response of academics and others to the Facebook experiment. What are the different perspectives on this experiment? What impact did the discovery of this experiment have on social media?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ46.1
constructive_questions.Details: Using the latest Statistical Abstract of the United States, find data on some aspect of media use in America that you find interesting. Print out the page with the data and turn it in with your discussion of what was interesting about the data. Then find data on media use in France, Japan, and Argentina to compare with the data about American media usage. What does this comparative data reveal about media usage in the countries involved? Did you learn anything interesting from making this comparative analysis?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ47.1
constructive_questions.Details: Find statistical data on the amount of television young children (ages 3–10) watch daily in America, France, Japan, and Argentina and the amount of advertising to which they are exposed. Does using a comparative approach offer important insights about children and the media in America?

constructive_questions.Name: CQ49.1
constructive_questions.Details: Find an example for one of 19 common thinking errors.
